p: You got to find a cobalt [sic] guy somewhere.
Yes, exactly.
Alright. So, it’s something that everybody is looking at is what you’re saying.
Yes.
Alright, thank you.
Thank you.
Thank you so much. And there was actually a situation in Chicago where they actually used AI and technology to actually track and make more efficient overtime.
Oh, wow.
It was a really interesting case which I’ll tell you about later, but yes. Okay. Sorry, Deputy Speaker?
Thank you. Hi.
Hello, Deputy Speaker.

Okay, I have a few questions. The first questions are on the MWBE report. So, as of January, your office issued the

annual report on MWBE procurement, and you found that MWBEs only account for five percent of the citywide procurement value, and that only eight percent of the value of contracts subject to MWBE participation goals were registered to MWBEs. Why did your MWBE report show such low numbers for the amount of city contract dollars going towards MWBE certified firms?

Thank you, Deputy Speaker. We actually now have a legal obligation in my office because the City Council passed a bill that requires us every year by January 31st to do a full report on MWBEs and how good our contracting is. It only covers mayoral agencies. So, I just want to put that on the table. So, Health + Hospitals isn’t covered. NYCHA’s not covered. EDC is not covered. It also only covers what’s in Passport. And there’s a problem with getting subcontractors registered into Passport. So, there’s some undercounting there. But having said that, I think the numbers are pretty stark, and they should serve as a wakeup call to us, and it’s very important to distinguish the number of contracts and the dollar value of contracts. If you only look at the number of contracts, the picture is a lot better. We had about 250,000 contracts and

purchase orders last year, and about 50,000 going to certified firms. So, that's about 25 percent, but that’s not dollar value. And the MWBE firms are getting much smaller contracts. The average contract for firms that are not certified is about $3.7 million. The average contract for certified MWBEs is only $750,000. So, you have to focus on the money, and when you do, you get a very disappointing number. That’s why we came out at five percent. And look, our job is to put that out there so we can rally and do better. And if you want, I can talk about ideas we can do that, but the numbers are pretty stark, and that should really upset all of us.
Thank you. Yes, I would love to talk to you about how we can improve the numbers going forward.
Yes.
I won’t ask you your thoughts now.
No.
But I will– I would love to talk to you about that.
Yeah.

But I will just ask a random question I thought about, because I know the state requires 30 percent MWBE contracting on all like government contracts. So, is the city not in compliance of the state law that requires 30 percent?
I think we’re governed by City Council laws.
Okay.
And I believe those are targets, and again–
[interposing] So, there’s no– which is a problem, right? Because there’s no real penalties–
[interposing] Yes.
if contractors don’t meet– which I thought the city was also going by 30 percent. I thought they adopted the state–
[interposing] Yes, but I believe it’s a target.
Okay.

And one of the reasons why we did the report and probably why the Council wanted to put it into law, is we go agency by agency. So, you look at every single agency and you

can compare who’s performing well and who’s not. And there’s a shockingly wide range of performance and MWBE contracting. So, a little bit of public exposure here and sunlight will help.
Okay. Yes. I held a roundtable with the former Comptroller to talk about MWBE related issues. I would love again to follow up with you on this.
Absolutely.

I don’t think we’ve been talking about it enough as a city, because there’s been so many advancements in terms of legislation, but the actual impact, I don’t really see significant impact. So, I would love to talk to you about that. Okay, a few other questions. Can you just walk me through in general the methodology your office uses to analyze the mayor’s Prelim? Like, any fiscal indicators or benchmarks you have?
And how we evaluated the mayor’s plan?
Yes.

The biggest effort we put into was really examining their revenue projections and we have 150-page report that’s

covering that and also the expense side. This is available online. And you know, we don’t take the mayor’s projections for granted. We want to interrogate it. And we came up with some lower numbers that in total mean about $1.8 billion less than we project in revenue in this fiscal year and the one ahead, and that’s one more challenge for us to overcome right now.

Okay. Does the Comptroller’s Office currently conduct any equity analysis of the city budget, specifically examples of how spending impacts different communities by race, income, or geographical location?

Well, the office has done many individual reports looking at that for given programs and agencies, but there’s not the kind of broad based equity impact requirement such as there is now for rezonings. But that’s something that I would love to work with you much more on.
Okay. And so I’m sure you’ll have a similar answer to this question, but I’m going to ask it anyways for the record.
Please do.
Which is are there any data sets or indicators that your office relies on to measure budget allocations– to measure whether or not budget allocations are equitably distributed across neighborhoods?
Geographically you mean?
Yes.
I don’t know if we’ve done a good geographic analysis on the budget, but I would– have we? But we would love to. And we’re going to partner with you, Deputy Speaker.
Yes, I look forward to working with your office.
Okay.
Because fortunately or unfortunately, I do plan to give you guys more work so you can properly–
[interposing] We love that.

analyze the budget for equity. It is really like the dying thing in my last four years, because New York City is so

significantly behind on how we analyze our budget. I mean, the process itself doesn’t even allow us to really analyze it in that way, particularly because of the units of appropriation issue. You can’t even really see what’s happening from agency to agency. So, I do look forward to working with you and getting your feedback to empower and encourage and require you all to do more of a deep dive around budget equity.
Likewise, Deputy Speaker. Thank you.
Nice, thank you. And next we have Council Member Wong followed by Council Member Mealy.
Thank you, Chair. Thank you, Comptroller.
Council Member, great to see you.

Nice to see you again. Before my questions, I want to say that as a budget director of the former Councilman Robert Holden, I can sit here all afternoon to tell you the bugs and the usability issues of Passport. So, if you have–
[interposing] I feel your pain, Council Member.
So, if you have your next meeting, we’d be glad to come and tell you–
Thank you.
my experience.
Thank you.

Okay, my first question is this. There are a lot of homeless shelters in my district and what I notice is they will fill them up to the seam and send the bill to the city every month. Here are number of occupants, you know, X number of residents. Send us a check. You know? Because of that payment model, there’s– I see very little incentive for them to get the homeless out of the system and into affordable housing. So, my question to you is that is it feasible for you to modify the contract so they could paid only when someone is out of the system and into a real housing unit? Only then that they’ll be paid based on the number of months they stay in the shelter. Would something you would consider?

I think there are a variety of performance metrics in the contracts, but

I’m not sure if they’re exactly like you described. Do you happen to know, Executive Director?

I mean, they are paid based on the number of– they have to provide services and food and– so they do pay based on the number of people that are residing there. I do believe– I know they used to have performance incentives for achieving placement rates. I don’t know the latest in terms–
[interposing] Right, but that is the framing. They’re supposed to place people in permanent housing.
I don’t see that happening, because if they place, there’s vacancies, and then they get paid less, right? So, there’s no–

[interposing] I think there’s always someone waiting to come and take that bed. But we will look into the state of those contracts. I’m all for having performance metrics. We have a very wide range of the quality of service providers amongst our homeless agencies, and there needs to be accountability so that all of them become better at having good metrics, and the contract is obviously one way to do that.
Okay. Yes, and I’ll follow up with you on the shelters.
Please.
I believe is just more interested in filling up rather than placing the homeless into housing.
Thank you.

Yeah. Here’s my second question, I still have time. Before we ask homeowners to pay more in taxes, do you believe the city has done enough to identify waste or control spending growth, and is there a Comptroller report that I could read about it where you could identify waste, or like controlled spending growth? Thank you.

Well, Council Member, look, as you’ve heard me say, I don’t think we sold raise property taxes for a variety of reasons, and I do think that we could do more to find some savings and efficiencies in the budget and to do some hard work on reconfiguring some of the programs. That should be our priority. I’m committed to doing that work with you. If you’re asking about a report from our office on waste, look, we audit every city

agency, that can uncover all manner of fraud and waste. And these are ongoing. We have many audits ongoing right now actually. They take a while. They could take a year or two or more, because there’s such intense work involved. But I think you’re referring to some sort of broader report on the state of waste–

[interposing] Yeah, no, like here are the programs that don’t work or here are the program that yield very little results, and those fundings should be reallocated. That’s the kind of report I’m looking for.

Yeah, and I think you’re right. We should judge just by how much we spend. We should just by what impact we get for the city and for New Yorkers. We don’t do that enough. I believe sometimes we just fund a program and walk away, and we got to ask what’s working. And you know, you rightly proposed we need performance metrics in our homeless shelter system so people get placed, and I agree with you, and I’d like to work with you on that.
Thank you. Thank you.
Thank you.

Great. Yes, I love performance metrics and being able to measure if something’s working or not. And next we have Council Member Avilés. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Thank you, Chair. Good to see you, Comptroller.
Likewise, Council Member. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: I guess I have a couple of different questions, and since I was in and out, it’s possible you’ve answered them already.

No problem. No problem. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: But I’d like to start with NYCHA. I was wondering if your office has put forward any recommendations and/or looked at PACT converted developments in terms of just general oversight?

Well, in the 2+ months I’ve been there, no. My predecessor Comptroller Lander did put out a report that was fairly critical. This is something that we’re extremely interested in. This is– it does appear the

current administration intends to continue at least in one prominent case in Chelsea, Elliot, Fulton Houses, and that might indicate that they’re open to it in other developments as well. So, some people are going to be looking at closely. You know as much about public housing as anyone in New York City, because obviously having chaired the committee, and boy, we’re not left with a lot of easy options here. And with the federal government that’s turned its back on us, with the state government that helps some, but not enough relative to the $80 billion we need to invest in the capital of these buildings, we’re going to have to look at greater solutions. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Sure.

And RAD/PACT is one of them. But yeah, we need to have– keep it under scrutiny, especially now that we have a number of developments that have been running already for a couple years, and we could look at how they’re doing. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: 100 percent. You know, I think, as you know, NYCHA currently has over 6,000 units sitting empty. Is your office– do you think you will be looking at that in the long-term

impacts of a growing number of units that are empty amidst the housing crisis?
Well, yes, I’m very worried about this. The turnaround time is getting longer and longer and longer between– COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: [interposing] And the numbers are growing.
Yeah, therefore, because it’s taking longer, you’re getting a bigger inventory which I think is now pushing 7,000 units. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Yes.
And in the middle of a housing crisis– COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: [interposing] With 175,000 people on a waiting list.

Yes. So, it’s unacceptable. We are pushing on that. I’m not sure if that would work for the timeline of an audit which tends to be slower, but I’d like to join with you and the Council to push very, very hard on that. We have got to get those apartments full. There’s also been reporting that now some people are breaking into them and living there which is a security issue. Of course, people are desperate. I get it, but this is

not acceptable. You got to get those apartments renovated and turned around faster and families in there as soon as possible. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Thank you. We’d love your help in making sure that happens.

You will have it, yes. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Similarly, I think we– there has been in terms of supportive housing, vacant supportive housing units is another deep concern where we understand there are thousands of supportive housing empty in the middle of a housing crisis is unacceptable.
This is a different issue, also very problematic, but I don’t think this is about a renovation challenge. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: No, it’s not, but–

[interposing] And it’s not even I think about the nonprofits. I think this is a bureaucracy which is too slow to get people identified and place. And again, we’re in the middle of a shortage on supportive units as well. This has to be sped up.

COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Yes. I couldn’t agree more. In terms of just shifting a little bit, commercial vacancies. I see in my district a growing number of commercial vacancies. I’m wondering if you have any suggestions. We know the impacts of these vacancies are really profound, and we’re hearing in Brooklyn that there’s 21.8 percentage. And so do you have any recommendations? Are you tracking that?

I’m very worried about this. When you have vacant storefronts, it zaps life from the neighborhood. It’s a public safety issue. It’s a public health issue. There’s so many secondary problems. We have very little data on this which is why I was excited to hear you have such a precise number in your community. So, thank you for doing that work. I would like to figure out a way to have a citywide data set to track this which we don’t currently have. Council Member Brewer actually has done some good analysis on the Upper West Side on Broadway. I think it required Council Member interns going block by block. So, I’m not sure if we can do that citywide. But I have some ideas, using technology to build this out. If we can get a good

number, we can track this, and it would help us focus attention on solving this problem. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Couldn’t agree with you more, and certainly the impacts innumerable, and certainly one of the main drivers is the rent is too damn high, particularly in commercial context.
Yes. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Do you think commercial rent stabilization could help support that?

Maybe. I think it’s more complicated than residential for a variety of reasons. I think we should be looking at it, though, but I think we have some underlying challenges that are beyond that, competition from the internet probably being the biggest. Cost being a major factor, of utilities, of real estate taxes. Here we are talking about that. So, look, for people who are complaining about retail storefronts, please don’t order your toothbrush online. Go to a store in the neighborhood and buy from a local merchant. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Heard. Thank you. Thank you, Comptroller.

You got it.

COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Thank you.

Alright, thank you. And I’m just going to go into a few more questions before we wrap it up. Going into the debt service savings. So, in the past 10 fiscal years the city has been able to identify at least $195 million in debt service savings annually with average annual savings exceeding $300 million. However, this year, OMB has only identified $156 million in savings thus far. And for example, our staff believe that the interest assumptions used by OMB are a bit unrealistic as projected interest rates are always higher than the actual rates, and right-sizing these rates would create savings including variable rate debt costs which would be felt immediately. So, do you believe that there are additional savings to be had in the debt service budget, because I know there’s differing–

[interposing] I am going to pass it to Francesco. I just want to– I want to caution you here that I’m not so sure that this is going to be an easy pot of money to find, partly because rates are set by conditions beyond our

control or by an event like a refinancing, and that we have not– we have decided that it would not be prudent to add more savings into our projections, but I’m going to have Francesco weigh in who’s more of an expert.

So, the city has traditionally recognized the savings at the time when they are– when there are refundings, for instance, and the city, you know, tends to set some assumptions that are a little more pessimistic than what it has– than realizes, right? That’s always been a buffer for the city. We have a couple of refundings coming up which are going to provide a few– you know, which are going to provide to resources. It is– how should I say it? It is not an amount of money that is large enough, and it’s not an amount of money that it’s current enough to–
[interposing] What’s your estimate for–
[interposing] We can get back to you with–
[interposing] Okay.

an estimate and we’ll speak to your staff. But this is

not– you know, it’s sort of like taking risk in the future, right, to have savings– to already take savings in the future where, you know, it’s not going to– it’s not going to change structurally the situation.

I mean, but– right. Well, I guess that’s what I’m curious to hear about more, because you know, even when I was doing, again, much, much smaller scale, but my nonprofit does service budgeting every year. You know, there usually are things that you can sort of find and dig into. So, I just wanted to get a sense of if you could provide more details on the type of savings that have been found in the past, and then also what role if any your office does play in finding those savings within the Comptroller's Office.

So, the Office of the Comptroller and the Office of Management and Budget, they work jointly on all of that issuances and identifying the bonds that need to be refunded to maximize the amount of refunding. What we do is we typically take the savings from the refundings and we pursue them aggressively and we spread them over the financial plan. This has been

long-standing policy that we’ve applied. And we realize the savings in the budget as we issue the bonds and we get those savings in the financial plan.

And then moving over to the interest earnings. Our council finance team believes that the city historically under-forecasts the interest earnings on its cash balances based on revenues generated so far, and we believe that there’s more money that OMB can recognize here, and also in FY 27 and in the out-years, as interest rates are expected to stay relatively elevated. In addition, there are a number of off-book entities with their own cash balances that earn interest that we should account for when balancing the budget, and so– like the RHBT and the Hudson Yards Infrastructure Corporation. Have you looked at interest earnings in the city’s cash balance?
Every day.
Yes.
I’m not kidding. So, we have– I’m sorry, Comptroller.

Well, let me just say big picture on that, then I’m going to pass it to you for the technical expertise. Look, this is all– we have what we call a short-term desk. This is money that needs to be incredibly liquid and has to be in very high-quality investments, and therefore, you're going to get a low interest rate. That’s the trade-off. You’re not going to get very high interest rate on something that has to be liquid. You can’t take on a lot of risks, and we have a whole team dedicated to our short-term desk and our Bureau of Asset Management, and I’m pretty confident that they’re getting the right risk return balance. Again, I would caution you that I don’t think this is a big pot of savings to be achieved, and now I’m going to pass it off to you.

Well, we have the treasurer for the city, I think, sitting all the way over there, and we work closely with them to do overnight [sic] investment of the city cash balances. Now, to the– those are done by the Office of the Comptroller. The– we also invest [inaudible] health benefit trust [sic] balance, and that’s based on investment guidelines that are set by

OMB, but the fact that we do it, it means that OMB sets guideline that, you know, require us to invest in short-term assets, right? And so, that’s a conversations that, you know, needs to be had. If there is an opportunity to have higher interest on those, that’s a– first, we need to change the guidelines and we wouldn't be able to do it, right, if it’s not short-term. This is not something that, you know, we would do in house at the Office of the Comptroller. HYIC [sic] manages its bond proceeds and the interest on those, and the Comptroller has no role in that.
ARe there steps the city could do to improve the revenue the city generates on its cash balances?

We– the Department of Finance has a forecast of cash balances. OMB does. We do every quarter publish– there are a couple of things. One, they’re very dependent on short-term interset rates. So, during the pandemic we had zero earnings and large cash balances, and now we have higher interest rates, and therefore higher income, but a trend of shrinking cash balances, right? So, the two things are sort of

like going in opposing directions. So, it really will depend for this year and the next what we see with the expense trajectory and with the revenue trajectory, right? So, that’s going to be crucial to understand where our cash balance is going to go. But there’s not a sense. We do offsets. We calculate offsets to the interest income in our report. So it’s part of, you know, when we come up with a re-estimate of the gap, that’s part of it, too. And we’d be glad to show you what our numbers are, and you know, the forecast of where the interest rates are going to be. So, you know, that’s also another margin of error. You know, is the fed going to tighten or loosen and how fast, right?

Right. And I know that cash balances can be tough because it is so fluid and it is moving around so quickly. But definitely whatever we can do to try to see how to increase, that would be great. And of course, Comptroller’s Office, you– the big responsibility you all have with our pension funds is obviously a huge thing. So, in terms of the pension annual returns, in Fiscal 2025, the city’s pensions systems achieved a 10.3 percent aggregate net return on investments, significantly

exceeding the seven percent actuarial assumption. So, can you please update the committee on the year-to-date returns for the city’s pension system?

I want to answer that, but I have to update you on some very serious breaking news related to our topic today which is Moody’s has just issued a report, and they are revising their outlook for us, which is very unusual, from stable to negative. This is not a bond downgrade, but it’s serious, and it should focus us on the challenge of these structural deficits that we’ve been speaking about. They cites this in their analysis. I want to say what I said earlier that our bond ratings are all stable, and we expect that to continue for the near future. We have a bond sale next week that we expect to go forward normally. But I do want you and us to absorb what just happened. This is the first time since the pandemic that Moody’s has had a negative revision in its outlook for us and it’s a reminder of the scale of the challenges ahead of us.
Sorry, just really quickly on that point. So, how’s that going to impact future borrowing?

I don’t think it has an immediate impact. It doesn’t change our bond rating but this can sometimes be a precursor to a bond downgrade. It doesn't necessarily mean it will be, but I think that should be considered a greater responsibility in the months ahead. Moody’s cited our action– our plan to take money out of our reserve funds during an otherwise strong economy. As I think I mentioned earlier, this generally serves as a warning sign to rating agencies. But again, a word of confidence here. We have not had our actual rating changed, and we don’t think that’s imminent and we don’t expect this will undermine our scheduled sale next week or in the near future which we do fully expect to be successful. You want to add anything?

Yeah. I mean, we need to be in the market rain or shine, right, because of the size of our capital plan and we need to issue billions of dollars every month. And you know, it’s just one of the considerations that the market will take into account and we will see, you know, where the interest rates are going to

be and the cost of borrowing. Certainly, it’s not a downgrade, right, but it’s a negative outlook, meaning that, you know, that Moody’s identified the structural spending problem. That's where the emphasis is. And if that is, you know, addressed in a similarly structural fashion, then the outlook will go back to stable, right? This is not, you know, a final determination, but certainly, you know, puts the accent on a further, you know, light.

No, it’s definitely something we need to look out for. And I think to reiterate the point, I think that’s why on the Council side we were very cautious or hesitant to say that we– you know, I mean, we’re very much against drawing down on the rainy day funds for this exact reason, because we were afraid that potentially this could have an impact on exactly what you’re mentioning. And so hopefully we’re able to figure out a way to, you know, dig a little deeper into the budget to figure out where there are cost savings, because I think– that’s a big concern that we’ve had from the beginning with the rainy day fund draw down. So, okay. Good to know.
Do you want me to speak on the pensions?
Oh, my gosh, yes. Sorry. Yeah, so going back to the pensions.

Because that’s better news. Our pensions are in good shape. We have at latest count I believe $316 billion in our five funds combined, and we have a much higher rate of funding than most other jurisdictions in America. We’re currently up to about 90 percent fully funded, and we’re on a path to get 100 percent fully funded through our payment plan by 2023. This is good news. And workers, city workers and retirees should feel good hearing those numbers– we have a goal on the rate of return, and our goal is to get seven percent as a long-term average. And we’ve been meeting that and beating it in recent year. Last year, I believe we had 10.3 percent, and this year I believe we’re at 8.3 percent. So we’re down a little bit because the market hasn’t performed as well so far, but even still, we’re above our benchmark. Really, though, the average retiree shouldn't even get so caught up in those numbers that I say, because are built for the long-term. We are perpetual investors. We are

universal investors. We are not day traders, and we have built a very, very robust diverse portfolio that does not live and die by the price of oil going up and down one day across all kinds of assets, private assets, public assets, equity, debt in America and countries around the world, and I’m really proud of our team, and I feel good about the state of our pensions today.

No, thank you for that, and I’m sure the rest of us are also very thankful for that. So, and what do– and I know you touched upon this earlier, but if you could just talk a little bit more about how the current economic challenges including possibly Iran war mean for the health of the city’s pension funds. And I know this is obviously a long-term game as mentioned. And how may these affect returns in the current year? Hopefully– you said it’s 8.3 or 8.6?
So far this year.
So far. And then so how do these potential things, how do you foresee it potentially impacting?

Look, I care a lot about– I care a lot about the economic impact of the war for New York City because of its– it’s pumping up fuel costs and inflation more broadly and also a variety of other critical supplies, 30 percent of the world’s fertilizer goes through the Strait of Hormuz, and this is going to be a blow to the U.S. economy. We’re already feeling it, arguably. And therefore, a blow to New York City’s economy. Having said that, the pension is a much longer view, and while obviously we monitor day to day, hour by hour developments in the markets, we’re somewhat protected from that kind of fluctuation because of how diverse and broad our asset base is. So, I would not want a retiree sitting at home seeing oil price spiking because of the war in Iran and worrying about their pension. Really, they’re protected from that kind of day to day impact.
And that's good. No, I just– thank you for saying that on the record, too, because I think as you mentioned it is a longer term game, so it’s good news for them.
Yeah.

And on cash balances, so we– I know we discussed this a little bit before, but on November 28th, 2025, the city’s unrestricted cash balance reached a seasonal low of $3 billion compared to $4.6 billion in FY 25 and $5.2 billion in FY 24. And while these lower balances are temporary, and typically the balances rebound with large inflows of revenue, they’re still a little concerning, and apparently these cash balances are not even as large as what we understand is the balances included in the assets for the rainy day fund. And so the Prelim Plan currently includes the use of nearly $1 billion of resources from the RDF to help balance the budget. So what is your benchmark for unrestricted cash balances being of concern?

Okay [inaudible] in the RDF and the health care and [inaudible] correct? Yeah. Right. So, the Retiree Health Benefits Trust, which I want to remind Council Members what that is, because I’m not sure people understand. That is to essentially have assets squirreled away for the health care that we’re going to retire– we’re going to provide retirees in the years ahead, and that’s a very large obligation.
Yep.

That it’s probably $100 billion. We have currently $5 billion in this fund for. Now, we’re not legally obligated– it’s not like the pension is not subject to state law, so it’s not an apples to apples comparison, but it’s not exactly a slush fund, and it’s why we should be a little bit cautious if we’re drawing it down, because it does serve another purpose. I’m going to refer to you, Francesco, on the other cash funds.
